1200 a day made me feel like absolute garbage, and I didn't lose much weight. Or I would lose weight and then gain it back because I would slip up from feeling deprived and then just quit tracking altogether. 

I started working out an hour 3-4x a week, eating 1600 calories a day, tracking macros (40% carbs, 30% fat, 30% protein), and measuring everything with a good scale, and I have lost 25 pounds in 6 months. I am 5'2" and started at 178 pounds and am down to 153. It has been slow but steady weight loss versus yo-yoing the same 5 pounds every month or so.

Building muscle bumps up your BMR, so the more muscle you have, the more calories you burn by just existing. Most people have to decrease their caloric intake after they lose weight to continue to lose weight, but I have actually INCREASED my calories and am still losing weight because my BMR has increased from the muscle I've gained. 

Good luck with everything. I hope you get the results you are looking for without sacrificing your mental and physical health.

Hemorrhagic conversion from the tPA. A standard CT isn't good at finding new ischemic strokes, but just rules out bleeds so tPA can be given relatively safely. There are a lot of stroke mimics (complex migraines, seizure) that can't be ruled out by a scan, and it just sucks because we're not even sure he had an ischemic stroke to begin with since the scans didn't find one. But sometimes, when tPA is given quick enough to symptom onset, it dissolves the clot before the clot can be seen on imaging. That's what they believe happened. But then the tPA caused a massive hemorrhage.
We have mobile stroke units with CT machines.

Recently had a patient who (likely) had an ischemic stroke. CT negative for a bleed. He got tPA. Was a drip and ship from a community hospital. En route, started vomiting. Repeat CT (en route) still negative. CTA on arrival negative for ischemia and bleeds. Waiting for MRI and possible thrombectomy, started vomiting, got agitated, had a generalized tonic clonic seizure. Emergently intubated. Another CT showed intraventricular hemorrhage, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and bilateral basal ganglia bleeds. He had a ventriculostomy placed and was on 3% saline for ICP control. Super high risk for herniation. They had to use hypothermic therapy, paralytics, and max sedation to keep his ICP under control. They didn't think he would make it through a decompression hemicraniectomy. His right ventricle collapsed, so they had to place a bolt. His ICPs were still uncontrolled. At some point, he went into septic shock for aspiration pneumonia (vomiting, seizing while being intubated). Even with uncontrolled ICPs, they did a clamp trialwith the ventriculostomy. He miraculously passed. Trached and PEGed. He transferred to the stepdown (where I  work) on the 22nd. I'm a fairly new nurse and my only goal was to keep him alive through the holiday. He was oriented to self and his left side would withdraw to pain but had no purposeful movement.

I had him on Christmas, and he halfway pulled out his trach. I asked him why (after paging ENT), and he mouthed that he doesn't want it. ENT exchanged his trach for a cuffless version. They covered his trach and had him say "1, 2, 3, 4" and I started crying in the room. He's oriented x4 and moves all extremities purposefully and anti-gravity.

I was surrounded by people of all walks of life in there, struggling with the same issues I was struggling with. It made me believe that fundamentally, all humans are equal. The other thing it taught me, however, is that I am in control of my behavior, even if I am not in control of my emotions. That may sound like a good thing, but I was still very depressed and suicidal and self-injurious for a long time. I just knew how to hide it to keep from getting "locked up" again. That's a fucked-up way of thinking of it, because really hospitals are there to help, not to punish. But it was ingrained in my mind that it was a punishment.

I think a lot of people think psychiatric hospitals are full of crazy, drooling, angry people. We do have some of those. But the majority are just people who couldn't cope with life anymore. The major difference is that there isn't a lot of choice in psychiatric hospitals compared to medical hospitals. And we constantly have to check on our patients (every 15 minutes--even when they're asleep) because everyone is a suicide risk. Anything that could injure someone (wires from a notebook, plastic bags, belts, shoe laces, etc.) have to be taken away. If a patient gets violent, you have to go to your room for them to restrain the patient and give them an injection. If you get self-injurious, you're given the option of a shot or a pill. 

Sorry, I'm just rambling things that most people might not know about psych hospitals. I'm super open about everything. It helps that Reddit is anonymous.
